title: Payments through one processor interface

blocks.text: The lesson's real-world abstraction: a `PaymentProcessor` interface, with a credit-card and a PayPal implementation. The rest of the application works with the interface and never needs to know how each method is processed.
`Payments.PaymentProcessor` is the lesson's interface with one query added:
Write the two implementations and one method written only against the interface:

items: `CreditCardProcessor(double limit)` accepts a payment when the amount is positive and the charges, with it, stay **at or below** the limit.
`PayPalProcessor(double balance)` accepts a payment when the amount is positive and **at most** the balance left; the balance goes down by it.
Either processor refuses (returns `false`, charges nothing) a zero or negative amount.
`refund(amount)` lowers the charges (PayPal also puts the amount back on the balance). Refunding more than has been charged throws `IllegalArgumentException` and changes nothing.
`Payments.payAll(PaymentProcessor processor, double... amounts)` tries each amount in order and returns how many were accepted.

blocks.text:
card = new CreditCardProcessor(100)
payAll(card, 30, 50, 40)  -> 2        card.charged() -> 80.0
payAll(card, 20)          -> 1        card.charged() -> 100.0   (exactly the limit)
paypal = new PayPalProcessor(60)
payAll(paypal, 20, 50)    -> 1        paypal.charged() -> 20.0
card.processPayment(0)    -> false
new CreditCardProcessor(100).refund(10) -> IllegalArgumentException

cases.says: payAll counts the accepted payments on a credit card with a limit and on a PayPal balance, written only against PaymentProcessor.
A payment that brings the card exactly to its limit, or spends the whole PayPal balance, is accepted.
A payment of zero or of a negative amount is refused by both processors and charges nothing.
Refunding more than was charged throws IllegalArgumentException; a full refund brings the charges back to zero.

concepts: Code written against an interface works with every implementation without knowing how each one works.
